summary: disease (Exposed group) is what the Relative risk calculator works out, and it gets there from the no disease, the disease and the relative risk. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Relative risk calculator work?
sections.html:
The Relative risk calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports disease (Exposed group) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the no disease (Exposed group), the disease (Control group), the no disease (Control group) and the relative risk.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Relative risk calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Disease=disease × no disease × relative risk ÷ (-disease × relative risk + disease + no disease)
Confidence level=((1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × z-score)
Lower confidence bound=(1 ÷ the exponential of (z-score × the square root of (-1 ÷ (disease + no disease) − 1 ÷ (disease + no disease) + 1 ÷ disease + 1 ÷ disease) − the natural log of (relative risk)))
Upper confidence bound=(the exponential of (z-score × the square root of (-1 ÷ (disease + no disease) − 1 ÷ (disease + no disease) + 1 ÷ disease + 1 ÷ disease) + the natural log of (relative risk)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Confidence level = 95 %. Straight away the calculator returns Z-score = 2.3262.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Z-score = 2.3262 should be roughly the size you expected from Confidence level = 95 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Relative risk calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the no disease, the disease and the relative risk — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Relative risk calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns disease (Exposed group), derived from the no disease, the disease and the relative risk. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Relative risk calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the no disease, the disease and the relative risk, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter confidence level in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Confidence level opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Z-score = 2.3262. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Relative risk calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
